A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OMP research, with matching objectives and retained simulation benchmarks. Text, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison. v1 ends with references and has no appendix; v2 includes Appendices A–E, which were also inspected.

before.justification: v1 reports original OMP success rates, component ablations and training curves on three Adroit and 34 Meta-World tasks.

after.justification: v2 retains original simulation results and adds physical-robot evaluations, synthetic experiments, memory measurements and action-horizon sensitivity results.

M1.justification: The cosine alignment loss, weighted reconstruction/dispersive/alignment objective, DDE approximation and single-step inference remain unchanged. Lcos becomes LDA, while OMP-JVP and OMP-DDE explicitly name the original full method and DDE variant already evaluated in v1.

E1.justification: The original 37 simulation tasks remain. v2 adds physical Place Bottle, Clean Table and Slip Ring tasks, plus synthetic multi-frequency regression and 2D velocity-optimization scenarios. Although Section 5.1 initially mentions four real-world tasks, Table 2, Figure 6 and Appendix D consistently document three.

E2.justification: The main simulation comparator set is retained. However, the convergence comparison changes: v1 Figure 4 includes SimpleDP3 and separate MP/MP+dis curves, whereas v2 Figure 5 includes DP3 and MP1 alongside FlowPolicy and OMP. The new physical-robot comparison reuses DP3, FlowPolicy and MP1.

E3.justification: New physical-robot protocols use 50 demonstrations per task, 20 trials with randomized object placement, and prediction/execution horizons of 16/8. Appendix E introduces horizon configurations 4/3, 8/4 and 16/8. The simulation description also replaces v1's four-state-history wording with a two-step observation history and specifies execution horizon 3; this reported revision does not establish that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds controlled spectral-bias and directional-starvation experiments in Figure 2, JVP-versus-DDE memory measurements across tasks and horizons in Table 3, and action-chunk sensitivity in Appendix E.1. The original tabulated loss and DDE ablations remain, merged into Table 1, while the convergence analysis is revised.

E5.justification: Reported simulation seeds change from 0, 1, 2 to 0, 10, 20. Both versions retain three runs and mean-plus-standard-deviation reporting, so no increase in repeated runs is established. The new real-world results report aggregate success rates without uncertainty estimates or repeated-training information.

E6.justification: Main simulation means remain unchanged, but aggregate standard deviations change: OMP 1.7 to 1.6, the dispersive-loss ablation 2.0 to 2.2, and the joint-loss ablation 2.5 to 2.6. Training curves are replaced. New physical-task rates are 80/75/70% for OMP versus 70/65/55% for MP1. Additional synthetic, memory and horizon results include long-horizon DDE outperforming JVP, 78.2% versus 76.6%. These additions do not establish improved retained simulation means.

T1.justification: Beyond v1's cosine-law and angular-gradient derivation, v2 adds a spectral-decay theorem and proof under a stationarity assumption, radial/tangential gradient analysis with a directional stiffness ratio, and a derivation of JVP activation-memory doubling. These substantial formal additions appear in Section 4.2 and Appendix B.

C1.justification: v2 makes identifying and overcoming spectral bias a central contribution, elevates gradient starvation and memory scaling in its contribution statements, and extends performance claims to physical robots. It removes v1's abstract emphasis on fixed dispersive-loss temperatures and improved few-shot generalization. The central directional-alignment and single-step-efficiency claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 newly interprets spectral filtering as inadequate fine-motion guidance and discusses memory scaling as a barrier to larger networks. Appendix E.1 attributes longer-horizon JVP degradation to compounding open-loop errors and interprets DDE's relative performance as greater long-horizon stability. The earlier DDE accuracy–memory tradeoff remains and receives substantially expanded discussion.

D1.justification: Appendices C–D add synthetic target-generation and evaluation procedures, direct output-vector optimization details, and physical-robot training and testing settings, summarized in Table 4. v2 also newly states that code and robot demonstration material accompany supplementary material; their actual availability cannot be established from the supplied PDFs.

R1.justification: Section 2 and new Appendix A substantially expand coverage of equivariant policies, one-step models, reinforcement learning, foundation models and world models, including OneDP, OpenVLA and Octo. DDE is newly connected to finite-difference research by Karakida et al. and motivated by Wang et al.'s Transition Models. Retained works' venue/year updates are bibliographic changes.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Related-work subsections reverse order, the method is reorganized around three theoretical barriers and two solution components, and experiments receive setup/performance subsections. An impact statement and Appendices A–E substantially extend the document's narrative structure.

P2.justification: v2 merges the original results and ablation tables, adds real-world, memory, hyperparameter and horizon tables, introduces synthetic-analysis plots and robot photographs, expands the environment montage, and redraws convergence curves with revised legends and step ranges. Figure 1 and the trajectory schematic are retained, with the latter renumbered.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses two important weaknesses of v1: simulation-only validation and unmeasured DDE memory-saving claims. Physical-robot comparisons with documented trial protocols, direct memory measurements and horizon sensitivity materially strengthen practical support. These gains outweigh reporting shortcomings, including missing real-world uncertainty and the Appendix E.1 claim of 82.3% medium-horizon JVP performance despite Table 5 reporting 80.7%. The stronger spectral-bias claims remain less directly supported because Figure 2 does not evaluate OMP's claimed correction.
